card.h1: How the Whole Sea Got Made: The Big Bang, for Sailing Folk
You already know the method: it's dead reckoning on the whole sky

ul.li: Dead reckoning: known speed, known heading, known time, and you can say where you were six hours ago without having been there
Cosmology works the same way. Measure how things move apart now, run the log backwards, get a date
Three soundings carry this whole voyage: stretched starlight, the light elements, and a glow soaking the entire sky

card.h1: Light from distant galaxies arrives stretched

ul.li: Space grows while the light is in flight, so the waves arrive longer than they left, shifted toward the red end
The farther the galaxy, the longer the crossing and the greater the stretch. That is the first sounding
Not everything flees. Close neighbors held by gravity keep their own courses, and Andromeda is closing on us

card.h1: It was not a blast, and it has no center

ul.li: Nothing exploded into empty space. Distances between galaxies grow everywhere at once, and every observer sees the same spreading in every direction
There is no port you could sail to and call the origin. It happened everywhere, including where your boots are
The model describes those growing distances. It claims no edge and no outside for space to grow into

card.h1: Run the log back and you get about 13.8 billion years

ul.li: If distances are growing now, matter was packed tighter then, and hotter the further back you reckon
Run that backwards and the sky's own log gives an age of about 13.8 billion years

card.p: Note. The Planck mission's fit: 13.797 billion years, give or take 23 million

card.h1: The first minutes forged helium, not hydrogen

ul.li: One second in: a soup of light and particles near ten billion degrees Celsius
Protons were already there, and most hydrogen nuclei are simply protons that never fused
Over the next few minutes neutrons fused with protons into deuterium, and deuterium into helium. By about five minutes it was too cool to fuse and the forge shut
Measured deuterium and helium match the predicted amounts closely. Second sounding

card.h1: 380,000 years on, the fog lifted and light ran free

ul.li: All that time it stayed too hot for nuclei to hold electrons. Loose electrons scattered light constantly, so the universe was a glowing fog
Then it cooled enough for nuclei to capture electrons and form neutral atoms. Light stopped being scattered and has travelled freely since
That is the oldest light any instrument can see. Earlier than it, the record is fog

card.h1: Two engineers found that light in 1965 while chasing a hiss

ul.li: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson, working a horn antenna at Holmdel, New Jersey, measured about 3.5 K more noise than expected
They checked their own equipment and their surroundings for the fault. The hiss stayed: the same in every direction, unpolarized, unchanged through the seasons
It was the fog-lifting light, cooled by expansion to a few degrees above absolute zero. Third sounding, and nobody was hunting it

card.h1: Three soundings agree, which is why the model holds
card.p: Each was measured independently. A rival account has to explain away all three.

ul.li: Distant galaxies' light arrives stretched — distances between them are growing
Deuterium and helium match the forge — both sit close to the predicted amounts
A glow fills the whole sky — and its faint ripples give the age

card.h1: Where the chart still runs blank

ul.li: The model runs from a fraction of a second onward. What set it off, and whether "before" is even a sensible word, lies outside what the evidence reaches
Lithium is the open sounding. The forge should have left roughly three times more lithium than astronomers find in the oldest stars, and nobody has settled why
An honest chart marks unsounded water as blank. The ancient glow keeps arriving from every direction while you stand on deck

brief.instruction: Plain, exact, and spoken aloud: a ship's navigator explaining the sky to a crew, not a professor and not a theme-park pirate. About 45 words per slide. The template holds median 60 words per card, p90 84, so 45 is a comfortable budget and no slide needs to reach 70; short is better than full here. Write it so a smart listener gets it the first time, aloud. Lead each line with the thing itself, not with a caveat. One qualification per slide at most, folded into the sentence it belongs to, never a row of disclaimers. The pirate frame is a lens for explaining, never a costume. Rules: no "arrr", "matey", "ye scurvy dog", "shiver me timbers", no dropped-g dialect spelling, no skulls or treasure. At most one or two nautical words per slide, and only where the word does real explanatory work: dead reckoning, log, sounding, chart, fog, crossing, neighbors. A slide that is all sea-talk and no physics has failed, and sea-themed filler is worse than plain prose. Every metaphor is followed inside the same slide by the literal thing it stands for, so the reader always leaves with the actual science: dead reckoning, then measuring expansion backwards; fog lifting, then neutral atoms forming. Titles state the finding in everyday words. Vary sentence length; short declaratives carry the surprising facts. No signposting ("Let's explore", "In this section"), no summary or inspirational closers, no "not just X, it's Y" constructions, no em dashes, and never the "Bold term: explanation" pattern on every line of a slide. Round numbers belong in the audience-facing copy: "about 13.8 billion years", "about five minutes", "a few degrees above absolute zero". Precise fits and uncertainties stay in a note or caption, exactly as written in the outline. Add no statistics, dates, names, or historical anecdotes that are not in the outline, and make no comparison between a measurement's precision and anything a sailor could do.

These are hard constraints, checked against sources. State them positively in the copy; do not turn them into a list of warnings, and do not soften or restore older wording. Recession applies to distant galaxies. Close, gravitationally bound neighbors are the exception and Andromeda approaches us. Say "distant galaxies" wherever stretched light or growing distance is described. Explain the stretch simply: space grows while the light is crossing, so its waves arrive longer. Do not call it a Doppler shift, do not use a passing-ship hail or siren analogy, and do not raise the scholarly debate about how to describe it. The plain stretching account is all this deck needs. Protons are primordial. Most ordinary hydrogen nuclei are single protons that were never fused. Never write that hydrogen nuclei were forged by fusing protons and neutrons; the fusing made deuterium, then helium, with a trace of lithium. Nuclei formed in the first minutes; neutral atoms formed roughly 380,000 years later, when nuclei captured electrons. Never collapse these into one event, and never say hydrogen atoms formed intact in the first minutes or have stayed intact since. The successful light-element evidence is deuterium and helium only. Do not add lithium to that agreement, and do not state a helium mass fraction as a measured property of the oldest stars. Lithium appears once, on the closing slide, as an unresolved gap: predicted lithium runs roughly three times what is observed in the oldest stars. Keep it to that, with no sigma figures and no proposed explanations. Make no claim about a physical edge, a center, or space growing into anything. No claim about who coined "Big Bang" or with what intent. No unqualified claim about unseen matter or energy; if either is ever mentioned, dark matter is mass known by its pull and dark energy is whatever accelerates the growth, and they are never merged into one thing. The antenna team checked their equipment and surroundings. Never say they ruled out the sky, since the signal is astronomical. Heavier elements were made later inside stars. Mention it only if a slide needs it, never as a new statistic.

Every slide is a navigator's plotting sheet: the template's flat navy field, white uniform-weight line work, numbered chips, hairline rules, and the single accent reserved for the one element under discussion. The conceit is a chart table, not a pirate-movie set. No skulls, treasure chests, parchment scrolls with burnt edges, or cartoon pirates anywhere. The explanatory white-line drawings are the heart of this deck, and four ideas deserve a substantial drawn treatment: a stretched light wave beside an unstretched one (the stretched-light slide), dots on a spreading surface all separating from each other with no center (the no-center slide), a timeline running from one second through five minutes to 380,000 years (the forge and the fog), and the horn antenna's beam picking up the same signal from every direction (the 1965 slide). Use the template's ledger, table, and spec-register furniture rather than plain bullets on the three-soundings slide and the closing blank-chart slide. The age slide's precise fit belongs in the template's note or caption register, set beneath the rounded figure. Give the cover and the closing slide open, quiet space. Photographs only in the template's white-outlined plates, and only where a real object carries the point: the Holmdel horn antenna on the 1965 slide, and deep-sky imagery on the cover. Everything else is line drawing or native data.

Aim for about 8 to 10 purposeful slides. Keep the good idea of learning through a voyage, but make the explanations enjoyable and direct, and make the science clear enough to explain aloud. This should read like a good short explanation to an intelligent pirate, not a collection of disclaimers. The pirate frame should matter without sacrificing clarity. Do not say EVERY galaxy recedes; nearby gravitationally bound systems are exceptions. Explain stretched wavelengths as space expands, without a side debate about the description of redshift. Avoid wording that suggests ordinary hydrogen nuclei were made by fusing protons and neutrons; most ordinary hydrogen nuclei are individual protons. Use deuterium and helium for the successful evidence; mention lithium only where its discrepancy stays honest and simple. Avoid claiming the oldest stars are universally 25% helium, or that every hydrogen atom formed as an intact atom in the first minutes and has stayed intact. Distinguish nuclei forming early from neutral atoms forming later. Use "about 13.8 billion years" in the copy and keep any precise fit or uncertainty in a note. Remove comparisons between the measurement's precision and sailors' noon positions. Do not say the antenna team ruled out the sky itself. Distinguish dark matter from dark energy if either is mentioned, or focus on questions about the earliest history instead. Do not confidently describe Hoyle's naming as an insult without a reliable source. Remove or qualify claims about a physical edge or whether space expands INTO anything. Do not dilute the science into sea-themed filler.
